bib.title: Adaptive-RAG: Learning to Adapt Retrieval-Augmented Large Language Models through Question Complexity

read.skipped: Reference list skimmed; Appendix Tables 7 and 8 (FLAN-T5-XXL and GPT-3.5 per dataset) only skimmed.

question: How can a retrieval-augmented QA system pick between no retrieval, single-step and multi-step retrieval per query, instead of one fixed strategy?
hypothesis: Simple retrieval strategies are less effective than the complex one while the complex one is much more expensive, so routing by query complexity should balance accuracy and cost.
contributions: Point out that real queries vary in complexity and existing RAG approaches are overly simple or complex.
Adapt retrieval-augmented LLMs to query complexity assessed by a classifier.
Show Adaptive-RAG is effective and efficient across diverse queries.

method.summary: A T5-Large classifier predicts a complexity label A/B/C for each query and routes it to no-retrieval, single-step retrieval, or the IRCoT multi-step loop. Training labels are collected automatically from which strategy answers correctly (simplest first) plus dataset inductive bias (single-hop -> B, multi-hop -> C).
method.task: open-domain QA (single-hop and multi-hop) with query-complexity routing

limits: Labels are automatically generated and may be wrong; the authors call it one specific instantiation.
Classifier is the simplest design; gap to oracle (F1 56.28 vs 46.94 with XL) shows room, and confusion is large (A->B about 47%).
Single run, no seeds or significance tests, due to cost.
Only three complexity levels; finer-grained levels left to future work.
BM25 only; QA only; 500 samples per dataset; Self-RAG baseline uses a different base LLM.
Silver labels cover only queries some strategy answers correctly; ablation shows silver-only labels generalise worse.
Ethics: offensive inputs or retrieved documents not handled.
